summary: Defines Augmented BNF, a compact notation many Internet specifications use to describe formal syntax. It covers naming rules, repetition, alternatives, order independence, and value ranges, and adds some core rule definitions. It was on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 5234.

plainLanguage.summary: ABNF is the notation that Internet specifications use to write down the exact shape of the text they accept. A rule gives a name to a pattern, such as the digits in a number, and other rules build on it. The RFC defines the notation itself, including the operators for alternatives, repetition and ranges, and then writes ABNF in ABNF so that a parser for the notation can be specified exactly.

questions: how do you write abnf rules
subtitle: The compact notation that most Internet specifications use to write down their syntax.

tldr.problem: Internet specifications constantly need to say exactly which strings of text are legal. Every writer invented their own way of saying it, so a reader had to learn a new notation with every document.
tldr.mechanism: ABNF is a form of Backus-Naur Form with rule naming, repetition, alternatives, order independence and value ranges added. A rule is a name, an equals sign and a list of elements, and the elements are built from concatenation, alternation, grouping, repetition and numeric or quoted terminals.
tldr.outcome: One notation that many specifications share, with a set of core rules such as DIGIT and ALPHA that a grammar can reuse. The document was a Draft Standard and has been replaced by RFC 5234.

facts.label: Bases for numeric terminals
facts.value: b for binary, d for decimal, x for hexadecimal

facts.value: A letter, then letters, digits and hyphens

facts.value: Case-insensitive, in the us-ascii character set

today: RFC 4234 was published in October 2005 as a Draft Standard and has been obsoleted by RFC 5234, which restates ABNF and adds a number of new core rules. It had itself obsoleted RFC 2234.

sections.title: What ABNF Is For
sections.content:
Internet technical specifications often need to define a formal syntax, and are free to employ whatever notation their authors deem useful. Over the years a modified version of Backus-Naur Form, called Augmented BNF, has been popular among many Internet specifications. It balances compactness and simplicity with reasonable representational power.

In the early days of the Arpanet, each specification contained its own definition of ABNF, including the email specifications RFC 733 and then RFC 822, which came to be the common citations for defining it. The current document separates those definitions so that a specification can refer to just the part it needs. Predictably, it also provides some modifications and enhancements. The differences between standard BNF and ABNF involve naming rules, repetition, alternatives, order-independence and value ranges.

The document also supplies rule definitions and encoding for a core lexical analyser of the type common to several Internet specifications. That core is in an appendix, provided as a convenience, and is separate from the meta-language defined in the body of the document and separate from its formal status. The changes from the previous version were small: a phrase about exact repetition was corrected, and some continuation comment lines were corrected to begin with the comment character.
sections.plainLanguage: Before this document, every specification that needed to define a text format also defined its own notation, usually by copying the one from the mail standards. This RFC pulls that notation out into a document of its own so that other specifications can point at it, and tidies it up at the same time.

sections.title: Rules, Names and Terminal Values
sections.content:
The name of a rule is the name itself: a sequence of characters beginning with an alphabetic character and followed by any combination of letters, digits and hyphens. Rule names are case-insensitive, so <rulename>, <Rulename> and <RULENAME> all refer to the same rule. Unlike original BNF, angle brackets are not required, though they may be used around a rule name wherever that helps a reader see it, typically in free-form prose or to distinguish partial rules that combine into a string with no white space between them.

A rule is defined as a name, an equals sign and one or more rule names or terminal specifications, ending with the end-of-line indicator. For visual ease, rule definitions are left aligned and continuation lines are indented.

Rules resolve into a string of terminal values, sometimes called characters, and in ABNF a character is merely a non-negative integer; in certain contexts a specific mapping of values into a character set, such as ASCII, is specified. Terminals are given as one or more numeric characters with the base stated explicitly: b for binary, d for decimal and x for hexadecimal. So %d13 and %x0D both mean carriage return, and %d13.10 means carriage return followed by line feed, the period separating characters within one value.

ABNF also allows literal text strings in quotation marks, which are interpreted as a concatenated set of printable characters. These strings are case-insensitive and use the us-ascii character set, so rulename = "abc" matches "abc", "Abc", "aBc" and every other mixture of cases. To specify a rule that is case sensitive, the characters have to be given individually, for example %d97 %d98 %d99 or %d97.98.99, which match only the lower-case string abc.
sections.plainLanguage: A rule is a name and a description of what it matches, written on one line. Names may use letters, digits and hyphens, and their case does not matter. The things a rule finally matches are numbers, where each number stands for one character, and the notation says which base the number is written in.

sections.title: The Operators
sections.content:
Writing elements one after another concatenates them, so foo bar foo matches the three characters produced by the rules foo, bar and foo. The RFC notes one important point about concatenation: there is history in Internet specifications of permitting linear white space, meaning space and horizontal tab, to be interspersed implicitly around major constructs, but this specification does not provide for that. Any grammar that wants white space around delimiters or string segments must specify it explicitly, often by putting it in the core rules it reuses.

Elements separated by a forward slash are alternatives, so foo / bar accepts either. A quoted string containing alphabetic characters is a special form of this: it stands for a non-terminal representing the set of all combinations of the contained characters in the given order, with any mixture of upper and lower case. Incremental alternatives, written =/, let a rule be defined in fragments, so a later definition adds to the set of alternatives of an earlier one; this is useful when independent specifications derive from the same parent rule set, as often happens with parameter lists.

A range of numeric values is written with a dash, so %x30-39 is the same as listing the ten values separately. Concatenated numeric values and numeric ranges cannot be mixed in one string: a numeric value either uses the dotted notation for concatenation or the dash notation for one range.

Elements in parentheses are treated as a single element whose contents are strictly ordered, so elem (foo / bar) blat matches elem foo blat or elem bar blat, while elem foo / bar blat matches elem foo or bar blat. The RFC strongly advises using the grouping notation rather than relying on a careful reading of bare alternatives when the alternatives consist of several elements, and recommends the form (elem foo) / (bar blat) to avoid misinterpretation by casual readers. Square brackets enclose an optional element sequence, and are equivalent to *1(foo bar). A semicolon starts a comment that continues to the end of the line.

Repetition has a full form with optional lower and upper bounds, where the defaults are zero and infinity. So *element allows any number including none, 1*element requires at least one, 3*3element allows exactly three, and 1*2element allows one or two. A rule written as n followed by an element is exactly n occurrences of it, so 2DIGIT is a two-digit number. The operator precedence, from tightest to loosest, is: strings and name formation, comment, value range, repetition, grouping and optional, concatenation, alternative.
sections.plainLanguage: The operators are the whole language. Writing two things side by side means they follow one another. A slash means either one or the other. A dash in a number gives a range. Brackets make a group that can be repeated, optionally, a fixed number of times, or not at all. Parentheses group elements so that the alternatives inside them apply as a unit.

sections.title: ABNF Written in ABNF
sections.content:
Section 4 of the RFC writes the notation in itself, so that a parser for it can be specified exactly. A rule list is one or more rules or blank lines. A rule is a rule name, a definition marker, elements and a newline, and it continues on the next line when that line begins with white space. The definition marker is either = for a basic rule or =/ for incremental alternatives. Elements are an alternation, and an alternation is a concatenation of repetitions separated by slashes, a concatenation is repetitions separated by white space, and a repetition is an optional repeat count followed by an element.

An element is a rule name, a group, an option, a character value, a numeric value or a prose value. A group is an alternation in parentheses and an option is an alternation in square brackets. A character value is a quoted string of space and visible characters, without the double quote itself. A numeric value is a percent sign followed by a binary, decimal or hexadecimal value, and each of those may be a series of concatenated values separated by periods or a single range. A prose value is a bracketed description to be used as a last resort when nothing else fits.

Two notes accompany the grammar. It requires a relatively strict formatting of rules, so a version of a ruleset included in a specification might need preprocessing before an ABNF parser can interpret it. And it uses the rules provided in the core appendix.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC describes the notation using the notation, so that a program that reads ABNF can be written from a precise description rather than from examples. The description is short: a rule is a name, a marker, elements and a newline, and the elements are built from the operators already described.

sections.title: Core Rules and Common Encoding
sections.content:
The appendix provides a convenient core for specific grammars, and the definitions may be used as a core set of rules. Certain basic rules are written in uppercase: ALPHA matches the characters A to Z and a to z; BIT matches 0 or 1; CHAR matches any 7-bit US-ASCII character except NUL; CR is carriage return and CRLF is the Internet standard newline; CTL matches the control characters; DIGIT matches 0 to 9; DQUOTE is the double quote; HEXDIG matches a digit or the letters A to F; HTAB is horizontal tab; LF is linefeed; LWSP is linear white space, which may continue past a newline; OCTET is any 8 bits of data; SP is a space; VCHAR is the visible printing characters; and WSP is a space or a horizontal tab.

The appendix also gives the common encoding. Externally, data are represented as network virtual ASCII, that is 7-bit US-ASCII in an 8-bit field with the high bit set to zero. A string of values is in network byte order, in which the higher-valued bytes are on the left-hand side and are sent over the network first.
sections.plainLanguage: The appendix is a toolbox of small rules that many grammars reuse: a digit, a letter, a space, a newline, and so on. It also fixes the usual external representation, which is 7-bit ASCII stored in a byte with the top bit clear, and larger values written first.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security section is one sentence: security is truly believed to be irrelevant to this document.

The reasoning follows from what the document is. ABNF is a notation for describing which strings are legal; it defines no protocol, no message format and no behaviour. The security of whatever a grammar describes is a property of that protocol, not of the notation, and a grammar that describes a format has to be read alongside the document that defines the format's own security properties.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC says security does not apply here, and it is right: this document only describes how to write down a set of legal strings. Whether those strings are safe to accept is a question for the specification that uses them.

viz.caption: THE ABNF OPERATORS AND WHAT THEY DO

items.label: Rule definition
items.desc: Separates the name of a rule from its definition, for example mumble = foo bar foo.

items.label: Incremental alternatives
items.desc: Adds to the set of alternatives of a rule defined earlier, so independent specifications can extend one parent rule set.

items.label: Alternatives
items.desc: Separates elements of which one is accepted, so foo / bar accepts either.

items.label: Sequence group
items.desc: Treats what is inside as one element whose contents are strictly ordered.

items.label: Optional sequence
items.desc: Encloses an element sequence that may be absent; the same as *1(foo bar).

items.label: Variable repetition
items.desc: Repeats an element, with optional lower and upper bounds whose defaults are zero and infinity.

items.label: Specific repetition
items.desc: Exactly n occurrences of the element, so 2DIGIT is a two-digit number.

items.label: Numeric terminals
items.desc: Decimal, hexadecimal and binary character values, with a period separating several characters in one value.

items.label: Value range
items.desc: A dash gives a range of values, so %x30-39 is the ten digits.

items.label: Comment
items.desc: Starts a comment that continues to the end of the line.
